title: A Better Covenant
sum: The writer states his main point: the high priest we have sits at God's right hand and serves in the true tent that the Lord pitched (8:1-2). Every high priest must offer something, but on earth Jesus would not be a priest at all, since the priests of the Law are already there, serving a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, the one Moses was told to build by the pattern shown him on the mountain (8:3-5).

Jesus' ministry is greater because the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises (8:6). If the first covenant had been faultless, God would not have promised a second. The writer then quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full: a new covenant, the law written on hearts, everyone knowing God, sins remembered no more (8:7-12). By saying 'new', God has made the first old, and what is aging is close to disappearing (8:13).
readings: The pattern from heaven

One reading takes the heavenly sanctuary as a real place, the original of which Moses built a copy. Jewish writings of the time also spoke of a sanctuary in heaven, and the Greek Wisdom of Solomon calls Solomon's temple 'a copy of the holy tent which you prepared from the beginning' (Wisdom of Solomon 9:8). Christ entered that heavenly original.
Shadow and reality

Another reading hears Greek philosophy: Plato taught that earthly things are copies of eternal forms, and Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish thinker of the first century, used that language for the Law and the tent. On this reading 'heavenly' means the true and lasting reality that the earthly rites only pointed to.
Promise and fulfillment

A third reading stresses time more than space: the tent was a shadow cast ahead by the good things to come (10:1). The movement is from promise (Jeremiah) to fulfillment (Christ), as in Paul's 'the shadow of what is to come' (Colossians 2:17).

views.H: The present tenses (priests 'are already there offering', 8:4; the copy they 'serve', 8:5; what is 'close to disappearing', 8:13) are read by some as signs that the Temple still stood, and that the letter was written before AD 70. Others reply that the writer describes the tent of the Pentateuch, not the Temple, and uses the present tense for what Scripture describes.
views.C: Critical scholars debate the background of 'copy and shadow': Platonic (through Philo) or Jewish apocalyptic, where the earthly temple copies a heavenly one. Many now see both at work. The quotation of Jeremiah follows the Septuagint closely, with small changes ('bring to completion' for 'arrange').
views.L: Chapter 8 is the hinge of the sermon: 'the main point' gathers up chapters 5-7, and the Jeremiah quotation frames what follows, since its last line (8:12) is quoted again in 10:17 to close the argument. The wordplay of 8:13 ('made old', 'made old and aging') answers 'new'.
views.J: Jeremiah's promise was made to 'the house of Israel and the house of Judah', and it puts God's law on the heart rather than doing away with it (8:10). How Christians have used 8:13 against Judaism is traced in Jesper Svartvik's study of the verse's reception ('Stumbling Block or Stepping Stone?', 2015). Christian readers who reject supersession point to Romans 11:29; the Second Vatican Council taught that the Jews 'should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures' (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catholic Catechism, speaking of the Old Testament as Scripture, says 'the Old Covenant has never been revoked' (paragraph 121). Calvin, by contrast, read the verse of the whole order of Moses 'as far as it was opposed to the dispensation of Christ'.
views.T: Christian tradition has read 8:1-6 with Psalm 110 as the heart of Christ's priesthood in heaven, and 8:8-12 at the Lord's Supper, where Jesus spoke of 'the new covenant' (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25).

deep.b: Hebrews never mentions the Temple in Jerusalem; it argues from the tent of Exodus. But it speaks in the present tense of priests who 'are already there offering' (8:4), of a first tent that 'still stood' (9:8), and of sacrifices that would have 'come to an end' if they worked (10:2). Readers who date the letter before AD 70 ask why, if the Temple had already been destroyed, the writer did not say so: it would have proved his point. Readers who date it later answer that the writer's subject is Scripture's tent, not the building, and that the Mishnah, compiled long after AD 70, still describes the Temple rites in the present. 8:13, 'close to disappearing', can be read either way. See also the book introduction.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's new-covenant promise twice (8:8-12; 10:16-17), and the two quotations frame the long argument about the sanctuary and the sacrifice. The first time, the stress falls on 'new' and the fault of the first covenant. The second time, the stress falls on the last line: 'I will never again remember their sins' (10:17), and so 'there is no more offering for sin' (10:18). Hebrews does not use the promise about the law written on hearts to set the law aside; it uses the promise of forgiveness to set aside the yearly offerings. The rest of the promise, a people who all know God, is assumed rather than argued. Paul uses the same prophecy in 2 Corinthians 3, and Jesus' words over the cup in Luke and Paul ('the new covenant, made in my blood') stand behind both.

echoes: Exodus 25:9, 40; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Psalm 110:1; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; 2 Corinthians 3:3-14; Colossians 2:17; Acts 7:44; Romans 11:29; Wisdom of Solomon 9:8

settings.what: The main point: the high priest of a better covenant
settings.by: The unnamed preacher of Hebrews, writing to a congregation he knew (13:19, 23)
settings.to: The congregation the sermon calls 'brothers' and later tradition titled 'to the Hebrews': believers who had come to faith through those who heard the Lord (2:3), had suffered loss and public shame (10:32-34), and were now tired, tempted to drift (2:1) and to stay away from the gatherings (10:25)
settings.when: after the long argument about Melchizedek (chapter 7), as the sermon reaches its center
settings.why: To show hearers who felt they had lost the visible things (a temple, a priesthood, a recognized people) that they already have a high priest serving in the real sanctuary, under a covenant God himself promised through Jeremiah. Knowing the hearers were tempted to look back makes the point plain: the old order was a copy and shadow, and God himself spoke of replacing it.
views: Many read the hearers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, drawn back toward the synagogue or the Temple's sacrifices. The whole argument from the priesthood and the Day of Atonement assumes hearers who knew and valued them.

Others note that Hebrews never mentions circumcision or Jews and Gentiles, and that Gentile converts also learned the Greek Old Testament. On this view the danger is weariness and shame, and the Levitical argument shows them what they already have.

title: Into the Sanctuary with His Own Blood
sum: The first covenant had rules for worship and an earthly sanctuary: a tent with two rooms, the holy place with the lampstand and the bread, and behind the second veil the most holy place with the gold incense altar and the ark (9:1-5). Priests went into the outer room every day, but into the inner room only the high priest, once a year, with blood. The Holy Spirit showed by this that the way into the sanctuary was not yet open while the first tent stood. Its offerings could not make the worshiper perfect in conscience (9:6-10).

Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, through the greater tent, and entered the sanctuary once for all with his own blood (9:11-12). If animal blood and the heifer's ashes cleanse the flesh, how much more will Christ's blood cleanse the conscience (9:13-14). His death set free those under the first covenant, as a will takes effect at a death; Moses too put the first covenant into force with blood (9:15-22). Christ entered heaven itself, not a copy, and appeared once at the completion of the ages to cancel sin; as people die once and then face judgment, he was offered once and will appear a second time for those waiting for him (9:23-28).
readings: The Day of Atonement fulfilled

The chapter follows the steps of Leviticus 16: the high priest alone, once a year, the blood, the inner room behind the veil, the people waiting outside. Hebrews maps each step onto Christ: he enters with his own blood, into heaven itself, once, and will come out again (9:28).
A covenant ratified by death

Another thread runs through the words covenant, death, blood and inheritance (9:15-22). Covenants were sealed with blood, and a will takes effect at a death. Christ's death both seals the new covenant and releases its inheritance to the heirs.
Conscience, not only the body

A third reading follows the contrast of flesh and conscience (9:9-10, 13-14): the old rites made people fit for worship outwardly; Christ's blood makes them clean inwardly, 'so that we may worship the living God'.

views.H: The furniture listed in 9:2-5 is that of the tent in Exodus, not the Second Temple, which had no ark (the Mishnah says a stone stood in its place, Mishnah Yoma 5:2). The red heifer rite (Numbers 19) was still known and discussed in the first century.
views.C: The placing of the incense altar inside the most holy place (9:4) is a famous difficulty: see the note. 9:16-17, where diathēkē means 'will', is debated: a deliberate play on the word, or 'covenant' throughout. 9:11 has a well-attested variant ('have come' or 'to come').
views.L: The chapter is built on contrasts: first tent and greater tent, made by hands and not of this creation, blood of goats and his own blood, every year and once for all, flesh and conscience, copies and the true. The word 'once' (hapax, ephapax) falls like a hammer in 9:7, 12, 26, 27, 28.
views.J: This is the most detailed use of Leviticus 16 in the New Testament. Jewish observance of Yom Kippur continued after the Temple fell, through fasting, confession and prayer, and the Mishnah tractate Yoma preserves the order of the high priest's service. Jewish readers note that Leviticus speaks of the Day as effective 'for all their sins' (Leviticus 16:34), where Hebrews says it could not perfect the conscience.
views.T: 9:14 ('through the eternal Spirit') has long been read as a Trinitarian verse. 9:27 is cited in teaching on death and judgment and against reincarnation. 9:28, with 10:12, stands at the center of the debate about the sacrifice of the Mass (see the card at chapter 10).

deep.b:
The Greek diathēkē has two senses. In ordinary Greek it was a will, the legal document by which a person left property to heirs at death. The Septuagint used it to translate the Hebrew berit, covenant. Hebrews uses it seventeen times; the Plain English Translation says 'covenant' everywhere except 9:16-17, where the writer's argument depends on the legal facts of a will: it must be proved that the maker has died; it is 'firm only in the case of the dead'.

Calvin took the passage as a deliberate use of the second sense, saying the Greek word 'includes both ideas' and that the writer 'reasons from the thing itself, and not from the word': the old covenant may be fitly compared to a testament because it was ratified by blood. Others hold that the writer never leaves the sense 'covenant': covenants were made by cutting animals in two (Genesis 15:9-18; Jeremiah 34:18-20), so 'the one who made it' must be represented by a death, and 'in the case of the dead' means 'over dead bodies'. A third group thinks the writer moves deliberately between both senses, as Paul does in Galatians 3:15-17. All agree on the conclusion of 9:18-22: no covenant without blood, no forgiveness without blood poured out.

deep.title: Where is the scapegoat? (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is Claude's suggestion, not a published reading. Hebrews follows Leviticus 16 closely, but never mentions the second goat, the one that carried the people's sins away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:20-22). Yet in 13:11-13 the writer stresses the part of the rite that happened 'outside the camp', where the bodies of the sin offerings were burned (Leviticus 16:27), and calls the readers to go out to Jesus there, 'carrying his disgrace'. Perhaps the writer saw Christ's death outside the city as doing both things at once: the blood carried in, and the sin carried out. The scapegoat's place is then taken by the call to follow Jesus outside the camp. Hebrews' silence about the second goat may be deliberate.

echoes: Exodus 24:3-8; Exodus 25-26; Exodus 30:1-10; Leviticus 16; Leviticus 17:11; Numbers 17:8-10; Numbers 19; 1 Kings 6:22; 1 Kings 8:9; Isaiah 53:12; Mark 14:24; Romans 3:25

settings.what: The earthly tent and its worship
settings.to: The same congregation, who knew the tent's arrangement from Exodus and Leviticus read in the Greek
settings.why: To make the hearers look at the old sanctuary through its own design: a closed inner room, entered once a year by one man. The arrangement itself was a 'parable' that the way to God was not yet open. For hearers tempted to return to that system, the point is that it never claimed to give what they now have.

settings.when: the climax of the sermon's exposition
settings.why: To set Christ's death in the frame of the Day of Atonement and the covenant at Sinai: one entry, with his own blood, into heaven itself, sealing a new covenant. For believers who had lost goods and honor (10:32-34), it promised a cleansed conscience now and his appearing again 'for their salvation'.

title: Once for All
sum: The law has only a shadow of the good things to come, so its yearly sacrifices can never make the worshipers perfect; if they could, they would have stopped. They only call sins to mind, for animal blood cannot take sins away (10:1-4). So Christ, coming into the world, speaks Psalm 40: God did not want sacrifices, but prepared a body for him, and he came to do God's will. By that will we have been made holy through the offering of his body once for all (10:5-10). The priests stand daily; Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down. The Spirit's words in Jeremiah close the argument: where sins are forgiven, there is no more offering for sin (10:11-18).

So, with boldness to enter the sanctuary through the veil of his flesh, let us come near, hold on to our confession, and stir one another to love, not abandoning our gatherings (10:19-25). Then the second great warning: for those who go on sinning willfully after knowing the truth, no sacrifice is left, only judgment; to trample the Son of God is worse than breaking Moses' law (10:26-31). Remember your earlier courage under insult and loss; do not throw away your boldness. 'My righteous one will live by faith' (10:32-39).
readings: The end of sacrifice

Read as an argument, the chapter concludes chapters 7-9: one priest, one offering, one sitting down. Psalm 40 shows that God always wanted obedience more than offerings, and Christ's obedient self-offering in a body fulfilled that will.
A call to draw near

Read as a sermon, the exposition exists for the exhortation. The hearers have open access to God (10:19-22), so they should come near, hold firm and gather together. The warning (10:26-31) and the encouragement (10:32-39) push from both sides.
Faith under pressure

Read in its setting, the chapter speaks to people who have already paid a price for their faith and are tired. The memory of their own past courage (10:32-34) and the promise of the coming one (10:37) prepare for the roll call of faith in chapter 11.

views.H: 10:32-34 describes the community's past: public insults, prison, property seized, but no deaths yet (12:4). Proposals for the occasion include the trouble in Rome under Claudius, when Jews were ordered to leave the city (Acts 18:2), before the deaths under Nero in AD 64.
views.C: Hebrews' text of Psalm 40 ('a body') agrees with the Septuagint in Swete's edition (mainly Codex Vaticanus) against the Hebrew ('ears'); the argument of 10:10 depends on it. Habakkuk 2:3-4 is quoted in a form close to the Septuagint in Swete's edition, with the clauses reversed and an article added ('the one who is coming'), so that the vision becomes a person.
views.L: 10:19-25 is one long Greek sentence built on three exhortations ('let us come near', 'let us keep a firm grip', 'let us pay attention'), matching faith, hope and love. The chapter turns from exposition to exhortation, from warning to encouragement, as 5:11-6:20 did.
views.J: The criticism of sacrifice in 10:5-8 comes from inside Israel's Scriptures (Psalm 40; Psalm 51:16-17; Hosea 6:6; 1 Samuel 15:22), and after the Temple fell Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai is remembered as saying that 'the practice of lovingkindness' is 'another means of atonement which is as effective', quoting Hosea 6:6 (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4). Jewish and Christian readers part over 10:9 ('he removes the first'), not over the prophets' point.
views.T: 10:10-14 is at the center of the Reformation debate over the sacrifice of the Mass (see the card). 10:22 is often read of baptism. 10:25 is cited for gathering for worship each week. 10:26-31 is read through each church's teaching on whether believers can fall away (see 6:4-6).

deep.h: One sacrifice: what the fathers said and how both sides used it
deep.b:
John Chrysostom, preaching on Hebrews 9:24-10:9, raised the obvious question for his own congregation: 'Do not we offer every day?' He answered: 'We offer indeed, but making a remembrance of His death, and this [remembrance] is one and not many.'

Both sides of the later dispute have cited these words. Catholic and Orthodox readers hear in them the Eucharist as the one sacrifice made present, not a new one. Protestant readers stress 'remembrance' and 'one and not many': the church does not add to Christ's offering but remembers it. The card below sets the churches' own statements side by side.

The warning of 10:26-31 repeats the shape of 6:4-8: people who have received 'the knowledge of the truth' (compare 'enlightened', 6:4; 10:32) and then turn away, for whom no way back is offered. Two things are new here. First, the writer names the act in the language of the Law: sinning 'by choice', like the Law's sins 'with a high hand' for which no offering was given (Numbers 15:30-31), in contrast with the sins of ignorance that the Day of Atonement covered (9:7). Second, the charge is spelled out: stamping on the Son of God, treating the covenant blood 'that made him holy' as common, insulting the Spirit of grace.

That phrase 'made him holy' is where readers divide. John Wesley's note says the person had been sanctified by the covenant's blood, so 'Christ died for him also, and he was at least justified once.' Calvin, at 10:26, limits the sin to those who 'willfully renounced fellowship with the Church' and Christ, and rejects 'Novatus and his sect', who used the verse to deny pardon to all who 'had fallen after baptism'. The church's long debate over whether Christians who denied the faith under persecution could be restored ran through this verse. The card on whether believers can fall away is at 6:4-6.

traditions.q: Christ offered 'one sacrifice for sins' (10:12) 'once for all' (10:10). Is the Mass or the Divine Liturgy a sacrifice?
views: Yes, one and the same sacrifice. The Eucharist 're-presents (makes present) the sacrifice of the cross', is its memorial and applies its fruit; Christ's sacrifice and the Eucharistic sacrifice are one, with the same victim, and 'only the manner of offering is different' (Catechism 1366-1367). The Council of Trent taught that 'the victim is one and the same, the same now offering by the ministry of priests' (session 22, chapter 2), and condemned the denial that a true and proper sacrifice is offered in the Mass (canon 1).

Yes. In the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom the priest prays to be made worthy to offer 'bloodless sacrifices' for the people, offers 'these gifts from Your own gifts in all and for all', and confesses to Christ: 'For You, Christ our God, are the Offerer and the Offered.' The offering is Christ's own, not a second sacrifice.

No, not as a sacrifice that earns forgiveness. The Augsburg Confession says the Mass 'is retained among us, and celebrated with the highest reverence', but it quotes Hebrews 10:10 and 10:14 ('by one offering He hath perfected forever them that are sanctified') and rejects the teaching that the Mass takes away the sins of the living and the dead 'by the outward act', since justification would then come from Masses and not from faith (article 24).

No. The Heidelberg Catechism says the Lord's Supper declares 'that all our sins are completely forgiven through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which he himself accomplished on the cross once for all', citing Hebrews 7:27; 9:12, 25-26; 10:10-18 (Q&A 80). Calvin, at 10:18, wrote that 'Christ's sacrifice is only one, and that it was offered for all', so that 'it is impious to repeat it'. The Christian Reformed Church in 2006 bracketed the answer's closing paragraphs, which call the Mass 'a condemnable idolatry', as not describing current Catholic teaching; the Reformed Church in America keeps the full text.

The Thirty-Nine Articles (Article 31): 'The Offering of Christ once made is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction, for all the sins of the whole world', and 'the sacrifices of Masses', in which the priest was said to offer Christ for the living and the dead, 'were blasphemous fables, and dangerous deceits.' This card gives the Articles only; Anglicans are not of one mind on how far the Eucharist may be called a sacrifice.

No. The Lord's Supper is 'a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church', eating the bread and drinking the cup, 'memorialize the death of the Redeemer' (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7).

echoes: Psalm 40:6-8; Psalm 110:1; Jeremiah 31:33-34; Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 32:35-36; Isaiah 26:11, 20; Habakkuk 2:3-4; Numbers 15:30-31; Romans 1:17; Romans 12:19; Galatians 3:11; Mark 15:38; 6:4-8

settings.what: One sacrifice for sins: Psalm 40 and Jeremiah 31
settings.to: The congregation the sermon calls 'brothers' and later tradition titled 'to the Hebrews': believers who had come to faith through those who heard the Lord (2:3), had suffered loss and public shame (10:32-34), and were now tired, tempted to drift (2:1) and to stay away from the gatherings (10:25)
settings.when: closing the long exposition of chapters 7-10
settings.why: To finish the argument that nothing more needs to be offered. For hearers tempted to go back to a system of repeated sacrifices, or who felt their faith lacked the visible rites of a temple, the sermon shows that Scripture itself (Psalm 40, Jeremiah 31) said the offerings would end in a better obedience and a final forgiveness.

settings.what: Come near, hold on, and the second warning
settings.to: The same congregation, some of whom had stopped coming to the gatherings (10:25)
settings.why: To move them to use the access they have: come near in worship, hold the confession, care for one another, keep meeting.
views: Some read the warning as aimed at those drifting toward open rejection of Christ, meant to stop them rather than to describe people already lost, since the writer adds 'we are not people of shrinking back' (10:39).
Many read the warning as describing a real possibility for genuine believers, to be taken with full seriousness.
Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, read it as one of the means God uses to keep his people, or as aimed at members who had never truly believed.

settings.to: The same congregation, who had suffered public insult, imprisonment of members and seizure of property after their conversion
settings.why: To encourage them by their own story: they had already endured more than they now face. Habakkuk's words about the coming one and the righteous who live by faith set up the roll call of chapter 11.

title: The Roll Call of Faith
sum: Faith is the assurance of what is hoped for and the proof of what cannot be seen; for it the people of long ago were approved (11:1-2). By faith we understand creation by God's word (11:3). Then the roll call: Abel, Enoch and Noah before the flood (11:4-7); Abraham's journey, his life in tents, and the promised son born to him and Sarah when they were past age (11:8-12). All these died without receiving the promises, confessing that they were foreigners on the earth looking for a better, heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be called their God (11:13-16).

Abraham offered Isaac, trusting God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed and looked ahead (11:17-22). Moses' parents hid him; Moses chose the disgrace of the Messiah over Egypt's treasures, kept the Passover and led Israel through the sea; Jericho fell and Rahab was spared (11:23-31). Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, of victories and rescues, and of those tortured, mocked, imprisoned, stoned, sawn in two, homeless and hunted, of whom the world was not worth (11:32-38). None received the promise, because God planned something better: they would not be made perfect without us (11:39-40).
readings: A history of Israel by faith

The chapter retells Israel's story from creation to the Maccabees (11:35), in order, through one lens. Every scene is chosen to show trust in what is unseen or still to come. It is a sermon on the whole Old Testament.
Examples for a tired church

Read in the setting of 10:32-39, the list answers the hearers' situation: these people lived as foreigners, lost what they had, faced shame and death, and did not receive what was promised in their lifetimes, yet held on. The congregation is invited to see itself in that line.
Faith as hope

Faith in Hebrews looks forward more than inward: it is trust in God's promise about the future and the unseen. This is close to Paul's use of Habakkuk 2:4, but not the same: Paul stresses faith as the way one is declared righteous; Hebrews stresses faith as endurance that does not shrink back.

views.H: The heroes of 11:35-38 point to the Maccabean martyrs (2 Maccabees 6-7) and to stories told about the prophets, such as the sawing of Isaiah, preserved in the Martyrdom of Isaiah and the Babylonian Talmud (Yevamot 49b). Lists of examples from Israel's history appear in other Jewish writings of the time, such as the praise of the ancestors in Sirach 44-50 and Mattathias' farewell in 1 Maccabees 2:51-60 ('Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations').
views.C: The chapter uses the Greek Old Testament throughout: Enoch 'pleased God' (Genesis 5:24), Jacob's 'staff' (Genesis 47:31), Moses a 'fine' child (Exodus 2:2). The variant at 11:11 (Abraham or Sarah as subject) and the omission or inclusion of 'they were tested' (11:37) divide the editions.
views.L: The repeated 'by faith' (pistei), eighteen times, is anaphora, the repetition of an opening word. The list speeds up at 11:32 ('time will run out on me') into short phrases. The chapter is framed by 'given a good witness' (11:2, 39).
views.J: Every figure is from Israel's Scriptures or Jewish tradition, and the faith praised is Israel's faith. Jewish readers recognize the form of Sirach's praise of the ancestors (Sirach 44-50). Abraham's offering of Isaac (11:17-19), the Akedah, is read in the synagogue at the New Year and stands at the heart of Jewish reflection on faithful obedience.
views.T: 11:1 has been read as a definition of faith by many traditions. The KJV's 'the substance of things hoped for' shaped much English-speaking discussion of the verse. 11:6 is cited for the necessity of faith to please God. 11:3 is cited for creation out of nothing. 11:35 is one of the places where readers see the New Testament drawing on 2 Maccabees, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold as Scripture.

deep.h: Who is in the list, and who is not
deep.b:
The roll call follows Scripture's order: Genesis (Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph), Exodus (Moses' parents, Moses, the Passover, the sea), Joshua (Jericho, Rahab), then a quick list from Judges and Samuel (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel) and the prophets, and finally the martyrs. Women appear: Sarah (11:11: in most editions she is the one who 'received power'; in the SBL's reading, which the Plain English Translation follows, she shares Abraham's faith), Moses' mother with his father (11:23), Rahab (11:31), and the women who received their dead (11:35). Some figures are missing who might be expected: Joshua is not named, nor Elijah, Daniel or Esther, though their stories stand behind 11:30, 11:33-34 and 11:37.

The list includes people with troubling stories (Jacob, Samson, Jephthah, Rahab the prostitute). Hebrews does not claim they were models in everything; it says God approved their faith. Several of the examples are of people who did not see the outcome: Abraham, the patriarchs who 'died still holding to faith', Joseph who spoke of an exodus he would not see, Moses who looked to a reward. That is the point for the hearers, who also had not yet received what was promised.

deep.h: Faith in Hebrews and in Paul
deep.b: Both Hebrews (10:38) and Paul (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11) quote Habakkuk 2:4, but in different forms and for different purposes. Paul quotes 'The righteous will live by faith' to show that God declares people righteous through faith, not by works of the law. Hebrews quotes 'my righteous one will live by faith', and then 'if he shrinks back', to call for endurance. Both include Abraham: Paul stresses his believing God's promise (Romans 4), Hebrews his obedience and journey (11:8-19). James uses Abraham and Rahab to show faith proved by works (James 2:21-25). Readers in every tradition have tried to hold the three together.

echoes: Genesis 4:3-10; Genesis 5:24; Genesis 6-9; Genesis 12:1-4; Genesis 15:5; Genesis 21:12; Genesis 22:1-19; Genesis 47:31; Genesis 50:24-25; Exodus 2:1-15; Exodus 12; Exodus 14; Joshua 2; Joshua 6; Judges 4-16; 1 Samuel 16-17; Daniel 3; Daniel 6; 1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:18-37; 2 Chronicles 24:20-22; 2 Maccabees 6-7; Sirach 44-50; Romans 4; James 2:21-25

settings.what: Faith described; the ancestors who lived as foreigners
settings.to: The congregation the sermon calls 'brothers' and later tradition titled 'to the Hebrews': believers who had come to faith through those who heard the Lord (2:3), had suffered loss and public shame (10:32-34), and were now tired, tempted to drift (2:1) and to stay away from the gatherings (10:25)
settings.when: right after 'we are people of faith' (10:39)
settings.why: To show hearers who felt like outsiders in their own city what faith had always looked like: trusting God's word about things unseen, living as foreigners, dying without the promise in hand. Knowing their losses (10:32-34) makes the picture of Abraham in tents, waiting for a city, a direct word to them.

To show faith choosing loss now for a reward later: Abraham giving up Isaac, Moses giving up Egypt's treasures and choosing 'the disgrace of the Messiah'. The hearers had been asked to accept disgrace for Christ (10:33; 13:13).

settings.to: The same congregation, who had not yet resisted 'to the point of blood' (12:4)
settings.when: the climax of the roll call
settings.why: To set the hearers' sufferings in a long line of faithful people, some rescued and some killed, and to tell them that those heroes are waiting for them: 'they would not be made perfect without us'. For a tired church the roll call ends not with them looking back but with the ancestors looking toward them.

title: From Sinai to Zion
sum: With so great a cloud of witnesses around us, let us throw off every weight and sin and run the race with endurance, eyes on Jesus, the Founder and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross and sat down at God's right hand. Think of him, so you do not grow weary; you have not yet resisted to the point of blood (12:1-4). Proverbs calls the readers sons: the Lord disciplines those he loves. Human fathers trained us for a short time; God trains us for our good, to share his holiness. Discipline hurts now and later yields the fruit of righteousness. So strengthen weak hands and knees and make level paths (12:5-13).

Pursue peace and holiness; let no one fall short of grace or be like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal and later found no place for repentance (12:14-17). You have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, trumpet and terrifying voice, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to angels in festival, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, Jesus the mediator, and the blood that speaks better than Abel (12:18-24). Do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven: he will shake earth and heaven once more, so that what cannot be shaken remains. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us worship with reverence, for our God is a devouring fire (12:25-29).
readings: The race and the stadium

The images are athletic: a cloud of witnesses, a race, a runner stripping off weights, training that hurts, weak knees, a level track. Jesus is the runner who finished first. The readers are mid-race and tired.
Two mountains

The chapter's center sets Sinai and Zion side by side. Sinai was physical, terrifying, a place to keep away from; Zion is heavenly, festive, a place of welcome. But the God is the same: the one who spoke from Sinai speaks from heaven, and he is still a devouring fire.
Esau and the birthright
Esau stands as a warning to the 'assembly of the firstborn': he traded his birthright for immediate relief. The hearers, tired and hungry for an easier life, must not do the same.

views.H: 'Not yet to the point of blood' (12:4) suggests no one in the congregation had been killed for the faith. The language of discipline draws on the household of the time, where fathers trained and punished sons, and an illegitimate son had no inheritance.
views.C: The Sinai description combines Exodus 19-20 and Deuteronomy 4-5 in the Greek, and 'I am full of terror' (12:21) comes from Deuteronomy 9:19, a different scene. Haggai 2:6 is quoted in a rearranged form. Editions divide over 'against himself' / 'against themselves' (12:3).
views.L: The chapter turns the roll call into a call to run: 'so then, we too'. 12:18-24 is a carefully built contrast of seven items for Sinai and of a festival list for Zion. The 'how much more' argument returns in 12:9 and 12:25.
views.J: Sinai and Zion are both holy mountains of Israel's faith. Jewish readers may hear 12:18-21 as setting Sinai below Zion; the writer's point is the greater nearness now given, and he keeps Sinai's God as the one who speaks (12:25-26). Rabbinic tradition also blackened Esau: the Babylonian Talmud says that on the day he sold the birthright he committed five sins, among them sexual sin (Bava Batra 16b).
views.T: 12:2 ('Founder and perfecter of faith') is a favorite text of devotion. 12:14 is cited in teaching on holiness. 12:22-24 is read of the communion of saints, the church on earth joined in worship with the church in heaven, and 12:23 in teaching on the state of the dead before the resurrection.

deep.h: The spirits of the righteous made perfect (12:23)
deep.b: Hebrews says the worshiping church has 'come near' to 'the spirits of righteous people who have been made perfect'. The faithful dead are spoken of as spirits, present in the heavenly city, already brought to the goal (the same verb as 11:40). Christians who hold that the souls of the faithful are with Christ between death and the resurrection cite the verse; so do those who teach that the church on earth and in heaven are one communion of saints. Those who teach that the dead rest unconscious until the resurrection read 'made perfect' as a statement of their secure standing with God. The verse does not describe what the dead experience; it tells the living whom they worship with.

Haggai promised that God would shake heaven and earth and the nations, and fill the rebuilt Temple with glory (Haggai 2:6-9). Hebrews reads Haggai's 'once more' as pointing to a final, one-time shaking in which everything made and temporary is removed and only the unshakable kingdom remains. Readers differ on whether this means the destruction of the created world, its purification and renewal, or the end of the old covenant's earthly order. The writer's application is simple: since the kingdom we are receiving cannot be shaken, give thanks and worship with reverence.

echoes: Proverbs 3:11-12; Isaiah 35:3; Proverbs 4:26; Deuteronomy 29:18; Genesis 25:29-34; Genesis 27:30-40; Exodus 19:12-25; Exodus 20:18-21; Deuteronomy 4:11-24; Deuteronomy 9:19; Psalm 2:6; Haggai 2:6; Genesis 4:10; Galatians 4:24-26; Revelation 14:1; Revelation 21:2

settings.what: Run the race; the discipline of sons
settings.to: The congregation the sermon calls 'brothers' and later tradition titled 'to the Hebrews': believers who had come to faith through those who heard the Lord (2:3), had suffered loss and public shame (10:32-34), and were now tired, tempted to drift (2:1) and to stay away from the gatherings (10:25)
settings.when: right after the roll call of faith
settings.why: To turn the examples of chapter 11 into a call to keep going, with Jesus as the one who ran the whole course. For people suffering for their faith and tempted to give up, Proverbs reframes their hardship as a father's training and a sign that they are true sons.

settings.what: Esau's warning; Sinai and Zion; the unshakable kingdom
settings.when: the final warning and the sermon's high point
settings.why: To warn against trading a birthright for momentary relief, and to show the hearers where they already stand in worship: not at a terrifying mountain they could not touch, but at the festival of the heavenly city. The last warning (12:25-29) is meant to keep them listening to the one who speaks from heaven.

title: Outside the Camp
sum: The sermon closes with practical instruction: keep loving one another, welcome strangers, remember prisoners and the mistreated, honor marriage, be free from love of money, trusting God's promise never to abandon (13:1-6). Remember the leaders who first preached to you and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever, so do not be carried off by strange teachings about foods (13:7-9).

We have an altar from which those who serve the tent may not eat. As the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate; so let us go out to him, bearing his disgrace, for here we have no lasting city (13:10-14). Our sacrifices are praise, doing good and sharing (13:15-16). Obey your leaders (13:17). The writer asks for prayer, gives a blessing in the name of the God of peace who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, calls the whole a 'word of exhortation', and sends news of Timothy and greetings from those from Italy (13:18-25).
readings: A sermon's practical close

Many sermons and letters of the time ended with short commands. Here they are tied to the sermon's themes: hospitality (Abraham, 13:2), prisoners (10:34), God's promise (13:5), the leaders' faith (chapter 11), the altar and the sacrifice (chapters 9-10).
Leaving the camp

The heart of the chapter is 13:10-14: the sacrifice of Christ took place outside the holy city, and believers must go to him there, accepting exclusion and shame. Some read this as leaving the synagogue and Temple; others as accepting social disgrace; others as pilgrims leaving every earthly city for the one to come.
The letter's ending

13:18-25 has the features of a letter: request for prayer, blessing, personal news, greetings. Some have thought chapter 13 was added to make the sermon a letter; most readers find its language tied to the rest of Hebrews.

views.H: 'Those from Italy' (13:24) and the mention of Timothy are the only clues to place and circle. Many favor Rome as the destination. The 'strange teachings about foods' (13:9) may concern Jewish food laws or meals connected with sacrifice.
views.C: Some scholars have questioned whether 13:1-25, or 13:22-25, belongs to the original; the links in vocabulary (13:10-14 with chapters 9-10; 'disgrace' with 11:26) lead most to treat it as original. The closing note in the Textus Receptus, 'written from Italy through Timothy', is a later scribe's guess.
views.L: The chapter moves from short commands to a theological core (13:10-14) and back to commands, then to a formal blessing (13:20-21) that gathers the sermon's words: covenant, blood, eternal, make perfect (fit out), will, pleasing.
views.J: The commands echo Jewish ethical teaching: hospitality like Abraham's, care for prisoners, faithfulness in marriage, contentment, the 'sacrifice of praise' and 'fruit of lips' from the Psalms and Hosea. The Talmud records the view that the daily prayers 'were instituted based on the daily offerings' (Berakhot 26b), and Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4 calls lovingkindness 'another means of atonement'. 'Outside the camp' is drawn straight from Leviticus 16:27.
views.T: 13:8 is a favorite confession of Christ's unchanging faithfulness. 13:10 ('we have an altar') is cited in the debate over whether the Lord's Supper is a sacrifice and the table an altar (see the note). 13:17 is read through each church's order of ministry. 13:20-21 is used widely as a closing blessing in worship.

deep.b: The verse sits in the middle of the argument about foods and the sin offering. The priests of the tent ate part of many sacrifices, but not the Day of Atonement sin offering, whose blood went into the sanctuary and whose body was burned outside the camp (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is that sin offering: so those who stay with the old system 'have no right to eat' from the Christian altar. What is the altar? Calvin read it of Christ and his sacrifice, saying 'the word altar includes sacrificing and the victim', with no reference to the Supper. Others read it of the cross. Others read it of the Eucharistic table, from which believers eat. The Catholic Catechism cites the verse for 'The altar of the New Covenant is the Lord's Cross', and adds that on the church's altar 'the sacrifice of the Cross is made present under sacramental signs' and that 'the altar is also the table of the Lord' (paragraph 1182). The writer's own sequence, from altar to 'outside the gate' to 'sacrifice of praise', moves from Christ's sacrifice to the believers' response.

echoes: Genesis 18:1-8; Genesis 19:1-3; Deuteronomy 31:6; Joshua 1:5; Psalm 118:6; Leviticus 16:27; Psalm 50:14; Hosea 14:2; Isaiah 63:11; Zechariah 9:11; John 19:17, 20; Acts 13:15; Acts 16:1-3; Matthew 25:35-36

settings.to: The congregation the sermon calls 'brothers' and later tradition titled 'to the Hebrews': believers who had come to faith through those who heard the Lord (2:3), had suffered loss and public shame (10:32-34), and were now tired, tempted to drift (2:1) and to stay away from the gatherings (10:25)
settings.when: at the close of the sermon
settings.why: To show what an unshakable kingdom (12:28) looks like in daily life: love, hospitality, care for prisoners, faithful marriage, contentment, trust in the leaders' faith. The center (13:10-14) tells hearers who felt the pull of the old sanctuary and its foods that their place is with Jesus outside the camp, and that their sacrifices are praise and generosity.
views: Many read the hearers as Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, drawn back toward the synagogue or the Temple's sacrifices. The whole argument from the priesthood and the Day of Atonement assumes hearers who knew and valued them.

Others note that Hebrews never mentions circumcision or Jews and Gentiles, and that Gentile converts also learned the Greek Old Testament. On this view the danger is weariness and shame, and the Levitical argument shows them what they already have.

settings.by: The writer, who knew Timothy and was kept away from the congregation for a time
settings.to: The same congregation and its leaders (13:24)
settings.when: as the sermon was sent, to be read aloud
settings.why: To join the congregation to the writer in prayer, to bless them, and to ask them to receive the 'word of exhortation' patiently. The greetings from 'those from Italy' and the news about Timothy tie the hearers to a wider circle of churches.
views: Italians away from home greet the church in Rome.
Christians in Italy greet a church elsewhere (Jerusalem, Alexandria and others have been proposed), as the later closing note in the Textus Receptus assumed.
